01-design-reviews/01-design-review-struc.title: 01 Design Review Structure
01-design-reviews/01-design-review-struc.description: PDR and CDR, and the interim sub-system design reviews for that matter, follow the same general structure. Comes down to the questions they are specifically asking. PDR is more about high-level architecture; CDR is more about specific designs meeting specific specifications. Define decision to be made Must define scope. Must be specific about what exactly is being reviewed: if we are concerned with reviewing mechanical designs (an engineer arm joint, for example), call the design review an Engineer Arm PDR/CDR, if we're concerned with the full design of the robot that includes embedded considerations then that needs to be understood. Initial criteria - is there enough material to hold a DR This is about determining whether a meeting is ready to happenIt's important that requirements are clearly defined. These are given in the form of competition rules, but the initial criteria are concerned with specific team decisions/goals. These need to exist clearly for this structure to work: Please have a clear set of robot specific requirements that you plan to meet for the year Initial criteria also needs the required CAD to exist, as well as prototypes or documentation of initial design decisions. Success criteria - things to pass review What's agreed upon to move onto the next phase of designing. For example, PDR would reach an agreement of: architecture of robot is valid able to/have reached major requirements Identify important interfaces (especially important when sharing chassis) realistic path towards CDR Prepare a review presentation - slide deck of materials The hardware teams should provide compiled information to me/Dag in form of short slide deck or document. This is combined with live view CAD and any prototypes. Review Lead/team presents designs and decisions. I'll ask questions against the requirements that are defined. Meeting shouldn't be a group redesign of some part-more about having a discussion on what we think needs updating should it pose risk later down the line. Closure Ending with one of three outcomes: Proceed: design can move on Proceed with specific actions Hold: some fundamental issue needs to be addressed This structure should be followed as close we can, but the scope of this process is ultimately up to the hardware leads in how much energy they want to dedicate to fitting their design process into this structure.ASU Example

01-design-reviews/02-scope-&-pm-role.htm.title: 02 Scope & PM Role
01-design-reviews/02-scope-&-pm-role.htm.description: General overview of the two major design reviews:What belongs in our PDR: Remember this is about correctness and feasibility, not at the detail of manufacturing This is point that has harmed us in the past-we go through the design process without stopping point to determine if it should reach a manufacturing stage PDR should show, for example: What robot must do/meeting our defined requirements Ultimately adhering to known comp requirements Concepts and exactly why one was selected Top level CAD --> refer here for more details Major subsystems and their interactions Mechanical & electrical interfaces!! Size, mass, CoG, loading, deflection--parameters like these should be considered here Prototyping/test benches Plans to reach CDR (CDR = manufacturable design) Leave this phase with the understanding that this given architecture will likely work, and any unresolved details have a path to completion.What belongs in our CDR: This is about having a design ready for building Should show, for example: Finalized onshape version/branch Complete assemblies/parts Materials/components to be purchased (BOM ready) Part drawings for manufacturing Assembly order Serviceability (I'm begging you) Fabrication plans Leave this phase with means to bring the design to manufacturing, and evidence that it will assemble and be integrated as expected.Doesn't necessarily mean every uncertainty is gone but they are at least recognized.My Role:I'll provide my specific advice from my experience as a designer, but I'm not going to pretend I know more about a subsystem than whoever's working on it. I'm responsible for asking questions that make it clear to us how this project is developing, and if it's developing in the correct direction. What requirement does this thing work towards? What assumptions exist What is the evidence that supports a design decision Interfaces and what downstream work does the thing affect What must be solved/tested before we trust a design to work

02-hardware-meetings/hardware-meeting-1-.title: 01 Prelim notes
02-hardware-meetings/hardware-meeting-1-.description:
Topics:
Shared robot projects
Design reviews What do hardware leads want from me outside of DRs CAD practices robot interfaces how sentry, standard, and hero will share designs
who will be responsible for standard chassis (sentry alone? standard helps? work needs to be split evenly) Hero: What projects will hero be concerned with, considering the above? design reviews decision about whether a design is mature enough to move onto next phase In the past, all design reviews were was a presentation of progress, going through CAD and the PM offers on the spot opinions. Implementing a PDR and CDR process seems like a good start towards something much more structure for this organization. Treating this the same way an actual company (NASA, for example) would, is asking way too much in my opinion. A PDR is deciding that the preliminary design can meets its requirements with acceptable risk and can move onto a more detailed design. A CDR decides that the design is officially mature enough for fabrication and testing. It's hard to have the expectation that hardware teams will go through a full preliminary design process, working towards the approval of a PDR, then move onto a new, more detailed process working towards a CDR. I think we should follow the structure of this--preliminary designs, then approval to a final design--but not with so much scrutiny as to make the whole thing fall apart. (*unless hardware leads are dedicated to this) specific activities:
design working session --> designers (hardware leads) solve a problem My involvement: when my experience and advice is useful technical peer review --> examine a mechanism or method My involvement: provide what knowledge I can and help ask the right questions PDR/CDR gate --> deciding whether a complete design is ready to move on My involvement: lead this process and make the readiness decision Following the structure of aerospace companies, reviews of progress take place before the PDR/CDR. We should definitely follow this structure, and this can either happen during bi-weekly PM meetings or my attendance at weekly hardware meetings.

03-cad-methodology/pm-commentary.html.title: PM Commentary
03-cad-methodology/pm-commentary.html.description:
Designing our robots to be parametric in CAD is literally fundamental to how the design review process works.Following a specific line of designing in CAD that you aren't able to backtrack will stop you at the PDR stage. Beginning your CAD process in such a way that every feature you make can be updated or removed is extremely important.
Starting with a defined set of relations and working off of them is common method of designing parametrically "master sketch" - hero is a great example of this Variable tables can set your most base level numerical parameters. This is really cool if you can get it working correctly. Every dimension of the frame of aerial is defined off a set of variables stored in a table. Allows you to adjust specific knobs of your design....

info_attractionForce.description: How much should linked nodes attract each other? This will make the graph appear more clustered.

info_linkLength.description: How long should the links between nodes be? The shorter the links the more connected nodes will cluster together.

info_repulsionForce.description: How much should nodes repel each other? This will make disconnected parts more spread out.

info_centralForce.description: How much should nodes be attracted to the center? This will make the graph appear more dense and circular.

info_edgePruning.description: Edges with a length above this threshold will not be rendered, however they will still contribute to the simulation. This can help large tangled graphs look more organised. Hovering over a node will still display these links.

info_minNodeRadius.description: How small should the smallest nodes be? The smaller a node is the less it will attract other nodes.

info_maxNodeRadius.description: How large should the largest nodes be? Nodes are sized by how many links they have. The larger a node is the more it will attract other nodes. This can be used to create a good grouping around the most important nodes.
